top_story: After Trump threatened in late March to destroy Iran’s power grid unless Tehran reopened the Strait of Hormuz, Tehran framed any concession as contingent on ending the US blockade and warned that pressure on its economy would widen the confrontation across the region. Iran briefly declared the waterway fully open on 18 April, but tied that opening to its unresolved standoff with Washington and then reversed course by 19 April, re-closing the strait after rejecting external nuclear demands and signaling that maritime access would remain hostage to coercive diplomacy. This stop-start control of the Gulf’s main energy corridor is now tightening risks for shipping, fuel markets, and Gulf populations whose livelihoods depend on stable trade flows. The immediate takeaway is that Hormuz has shifted from a bargaining chip to an active theater of escalation, with civilians and regional economies absorbing the costs of a US-Iran deadlock.
